comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/title: Legal gospel vs relational gospel (gospel of union)
comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/summar: Two broad ways of framing the good news that cut across denominations. The legal/forensic framework sees God first as righteous Judge and Lawgiver and the gospel as the verdict of acquittal secured by Christ’s substitution; the relational/participatory/union framework sees God first as Father, Son and Spirit in communion and the gospel as humanity’s inclusion, healing and adoption in the incarnate Son. Both claim Paul, Calvin and the "in Christ" texts; many theologians hold elements of both.
comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/rows/0: Holy Lawgiver and Judge who is also loving Father; justice and love are equally ultimate attributes of the one God.
Father, Son and Spirit in eternal communion; God’s love and fatherhood are primary, and justice is the righteousness of that love.
comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/rows/1: Creation and covenant
A covenant of works with Adam as federal head (Westminster 7.2), followed by a covenant of grace in Christ.
One covenant of grace from the beginning; humanity created in and for the Son (Col 1:16). J. B. Torrance warns against turning covenant into contract.
comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/rows/2: Guilt and condemnation before God’s law; Adam’s sin imputed; corruption of nature as its penalty.
Alienation, bondage, corruption and death; a broken relationship and a blinded identity — including real guilt, but not reducible to it.
comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/rows/3: Necessary so that a sinless human substitute could obey the law and bear its penalty.
Itself saving: "what is not assumed is not healed". The Son unites all humanity to himself and heals it from within.
comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/rows/4: Penal substitution: Christ bears the penalty of sin in place of his people, satisfying divine justice.
Christ’s vicarious self-offering in our humanity: the death of the old Adam, a "perfect Amen" to the Father’s judgement (Campbell), victory over death.
comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/rows/5: God’s holy, judicial opposition to sin and sinners, propitiated by Christ’s sacrifice.
The resistance of God’s love to all that destroys his children; not something that must be changed into love, since the cross flows from love.
comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/rows/6: A forensic declaration: sins pardoned and Christ’s righteousness imputed, once for all, through faith alone.
Grounded in Christ’s own justified humanity; we are justified because we are in him. Many affirm a forensic dimension within union (Calvin, Torrance).
comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/rows/7: The God-given instrument by which an individual receives Christ and his benefits; without faith, no saving benefit.
The Spirit-given participation in Christ’s own faith and obedience; in stronger forms, awakening to and agreeing with what is already true (du Toit, Kruger).
comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/rows/8: Scope: inclusion of humanity in Christ
Christ represents the elect (definite atonement) or provides for all conditionally (Arminian/Amyraldian forms); inclusion follows faith.
Christ assumed the humanity of all; all are objectively included in his death and resurrection (2 Cor 5:14). Subjective realisation by the Spirit through faith.
comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/rows/9: God’s eternal decree choosing particular persons to salvation in Christ (Westminster 3; Dort).
Barth: Jesus Christ is the electing God and the elected man; all humanity is elected in him, and he bore the rejection.
comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/rows/1: Assurance
Rests on the promise of the gospel and the finished work; confirmed by the Spirit’s witness and the fruits of faith (sometimes leading to introspection).
Rests on who Christ is for all humanity; believers look away from their faith to Christ’s faith and finished work (McLeod Campbell’s concern from Row, 1820s).
Calvin’s place
Calvin taught justification as "the principal hinge" of religion, imputation, penal substitution and predestination; federal theology developed his thought faithfully.
Calvin made union with Christ primary (Institutes III.1.1; III.11.10): justification and sanctification as a "double grace" from union; later federal Calvinism narrowed him.
Paul’s "in Christ"
Chiefly representative and covenantal: believers are in Christ as their federal head and mystically united to him by faith and the Spirit.
Ontological and participatory: humanity’s being has been gathered up in Christ (Eph 1:10); "in Christ" names the new reality of all creation.
Sanctification
A distinct, progressive work of the Spirit following justification, driven by gratitude and the third use of the law.
Participation in Christ’s already-sanctified humanity; becoming who we are in him; growth in communion rather than performance.
The universalism question
Rejected: only those who believe are saved; hell is real (usually eternal conscious punishment).

Divided: Torrance and most academics reject universalism as a system; Barth left it open; some popular proponents are hopeful or convinced universalists, while others insist on the possibility of final refusal.
Key texts
Romans 3:21-26; 4:1-8; 5:12-21; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:10-14; Philippians 3:9.
John 1:1-18; 14:20; 17:21-26; 2 Corinthians 5:14-19; Ephesians 1:3-10; 2:5-6; Colossians 1:15-20; 2 Peter 1:4.
Historic and modern representatives
Westminster Standards, John Owen, Francis Turretin, Jonathan Edwards, Charles Hodge, B. B. Warfield, J. I. Packer, R. C. Sproul, John Piper.
Irenaeus, Athanasius, Eastern theosis, Calvin (on union), John McLeod Campbell, Karl Barth, T. F. and J. B. Torrance, C. Baxter Kruger, Francois du Toit, grace-message preachers.
comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/overla: Both confess salvation by grace alone through Christ alone, and the full deity and humanity of Christ.
Both claim the apostle Paul and the "in Christ" texts as foundational.
Both claim John Calvin, who held union with Christ and forensic justification together.
Both affirm that Christ acted as our substitute and representative, though they interpret it differently.
Many Reformed theologians (Calvin, Owen on communion with God, modern "union with Christ" scholars) integrate both frameworks.
Both are Trinitarian and reject Pelagian accounts of salvation.
comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/differ: Whether God’s relation to humanity is fundamentally legal (covenant of works) or filial (Father-Son).
Whether all humanity is objectively included in Christ’s incarnation and death, or only the elect/believers.
The nature of divine wrath: judicial hostility to be propitiated, or love’s opposition to evil.
The role of faith: instrument that receives, or participation/awakening that acknowledges.
How to read Calvin, federal theology and the Westminster tradition.
comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/critiq: J. B. Torrance: federal theology turns covenant into contract and makes grace conditional.
John McLeod Campbell: it makes God’s fatherhood secondary to his justice and leaves anxious believers seeking evidence of election.
Eastern Orthodox: it reduces salvation to status and neglects healing and deification.
New Perspective scholars: it imports Reformation questions into Paul.
Pastoral critics: it can foster fear-based preaching and introspective assurance.
Federal theologians: it downplays guilt, divine justice and the necessity of personal faith and repentance.
Many Reformed historians (Muller, Fesko): the Torrances misrepresent federal theology and Calvin.
Evangelical critics: inclusion theology in its popular forms (Kruger, du Toit, some grace preachers) tends toward universalism and an unconditional gospel that removes the call to repent.
Orthodox observers: modern Western inclusion differs from patristic theosis, which is ascetic, sacramental and synergistic.
Critics of "hyper-grace": it can neglect confession of sin and moral exhortation.
comparisons/legal-vs-union-gospel/practi: Law then gospel: diagnose guilt, proclaim Christ’s substitution, call for repentance and faith.
Announce who people already are in Christ and invite them to see, believe and live it; exhortation flows from the indicative.
Look to Christ’s finished work and promise, confirmed by the Spirit and the fruit of faith.
Look away from one’s own faith to Christ’s faith and vicarious humanity; assurance is of the essence of believing the gospel.
Urgent call to flee coming wrath and receive Christ; conversion as a decisive transfer from condemnation to justification.
Telling people the good news of their inclusion and adoption, and calling them to awaken to it; less emphasis on crisis decision.
Applying forgiveness to guilty consciences; discipline and accountability under God’s law.
Healing of identity, shame and broken relationships; emphasis on belonging and the Father’s love.
Worship as grateful response to God’s saving acts; sacraments as signs and seals of the covenant.
Worship as participation by the Spirit in the Son’s own worship of the Father (J. B. Torrance); sacraments as participation in Christ.
